strengths: Comprehensive and systematic treatment of the online fair division problem across multiple information regimes (no information, normalization information, frequency predictions, and identical valuations) and multiple fairness notions (EF1, EFX, PROP1, MMS and their approximations), providing a fairly complete picture of the landscape.

The meta-algorithm for frequency predictions (Theorem 5.1) is a genuinely elegant and general contribution: it shows that any offline-achievable 'share-based' fairness guarantee can be matched online given frequency predictions, unifying several existing results (MMS, EFX for two agents) under one framework via a clean reduction using identically-ordered valuation profiles and picking sequences.
The paper corrects an error in a previous published result (Kahana and Hazon 2023's claimed PROP1 impossibility), demonstrating careful scholarship and attention to technical correctness.

Several tight bounds are established (e.g., the golden-ratio-related (√5-1)/2-EFX bound for identical valuations with normalization information, matching upper and lower bounds), and the results nicely interpolate between known impossibility and possibility results in the literature (e.g., improving on Zhou et al. 2023's 0.5-MMS bound via frequency predictions).

Clear connections are drawn to adjacent literatures (online scheduling, learning-augmented algorithms, online matching/knapsack/bin-packing with predictions), situating the contribution well within the broader online algorithms context.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical validation or experiments; while acceptable for a theory contribution, it may have limited direct relevance/appeal to the broader ICML audience compared to venues focused on algorithmic game theory/fair division (e.g., EC, AAMAS, IJCAI, AAAI).

The 'frequency predictions' model assumes perfect (noiseless) predictions throughout, in contrast to the broader learning-augmented algorithms literature (explicitly cited by the authors) that typically studies robustness/consistency trade-offs under prediction error; this limits the novelty of the predictive framing and is left entirely as future work rather than being addressed even partially.

Several important questions are left open (e.g., approximating PROP1 without information, whether EF1 is achievable with frequency predictions for n≥3), which is reasonable but means the picture painted by the paper, while broad, is not fully complete, and some settings (e.g., n≥3 under frequency predictions for weaker notions) are under-explored relative to the n=2 case.

The presentation is extremely dense and proof-heavy, with many long case-based adversarial constructions; the main text would benefit from more high-level intuition/proof sketches summarizing why particular constants (e.g., K, K^2, K^3 sequences) work, as the current write-up is challenging to follow and largely repeats similar-looking adversarial arguments across many theorems.

No discussion of computational efficiency/tractability of the proposed algorithms (e.g., runtime of Algorithm 1, Algorithm 2 with the leximin++ cut-and-choose subroutine) is given, which would be relevant for an ML/algorithms audience interested in practical applicability.

strengths: The paper provides a fairly comprehensive theoretical treatment of online fair division across multiple fairness notions (EF, EF1, EFX, PROP1, MMS) and multiple information regimes (no information, normalization information, frequency predictions, identical valuations), producing a coherent taxonomy of possibility/impossibility results.

Several proofs are technically careful and non-trivial, e.g., the general meta-algorithm (Theorem 5.1) showing that any single-shot 'share-based' fairness guarantee can be ported to the online setting with frequency predictions via a picking-sequence argument, and the tight golden-ratio-related EFX bound for identical valuations with normalization information (Theorem 6.3).

The authors identify and correct an error in a previously published claim (Kahana and Hazon, 2023, Thm. 13) regarding PROP1 impossibility, which is a useful contribution to the literature's technical correctness.
The related work section is thorough, carefully situating the contribution relative to learning-augmented online allocation, semi-online scheduling, and other online social choice literature.
weaknesses: Poor fit for the ICML main research track: the paper is a purely combinatorial/game-theoretic fair-division theory paper with no learning component, no data, no experiments, and no empirical validation of any kind. Despite borrowing the term 'frequency predictions' from the learning-augmented algorithms literature, the paper does not analyze robustness to prediction error, consistency/robustness trade-offs, or any statistical/learning aspect—predictions are simply exact oracle knowledge of the future multiset of values, which is a strong assumption rather than a genuine ML-relevant contribution. This substantially undercuts the paper's relevance and significance for an ICML audience, who would expect at least some connection to learning, estimation, or empirical demonstration.

The 'frequency prediction' model, which assumes exact knowledge of the full multiset of future valuations (including the number of remaining goods), is very strong side information—arguably close to full offline knowledge modulo arrival order—making the central meta-algorithm result (matching offline single-shot guarantees) somewhat less surprising than the framing suggests; the paper does not discuss how realistic or acquirable this information would be in practice, nor motivate it with any real application data.

The paper is very proof-heavy and dense, with long adversarial-instance case analyses that are difficult to parse; there is little intuition-building or unifying insight offered between the numerous individual results, which hurts presentation and accessibility.

Several central questions are left unresolved (e.g., approximating PROP1 without information, whether EF1 is achievable with frequency predictions for n≥3), and some of the achieved results (e.g., the normalization-information algorithm in Section 4) are incremental generalizations/modifications of an existing algorithm (Zhou et al. 2023), somewhat limiting the paper's novelty.

The promised extension to noisy/imperfect predictions (a natural and important question given the 'predictions' framing borrowed from learning-augmented algorithms) is explicitly deferred to future work, leaving the core motivation for using ML-style terminology largely unrealized within this submission.

strengths: The paper provides a comprehensive and systematic theoretical treatment of online fair division across multiple fairness notions (EF1, EFX, PROP1, MMS) and multiple information regimes (no information, normalization information, frequency predictions, and identical valuations), giving a clear map of what is and isn't achievable.

Theorem 5.1 (the meta-algorithm reduction from offline share-based fairness guarantees to online algorithms with frequency predictions) is an elegant and fairly general result that unifies several existing offline guarantees (MMS, RRS, MXS) into the online setting, and is a genuinely novel conceptual contribution.

The paper carefully corrects an error in prior work (Kahana and Hazon 2023's PROP1 impossibility claim), providing a counterexample and identifying exactly where the earlier proof's induction fails — this is a valuable service to the literature.

The impossibility results are proved via carefully constructed adversarial instances with clean parametrized limiting arguments (e.g., letting K or ε go to extremes), and are generally rigorous and easy to verify.

Several of the positive results come with matching tight lower bounds (e.g., the golden-ratio-related (√5-1)/2-EFX bound for identical valuations with normalization information), which strengthens the completeness of the characterization.

The related work section is thorough, carefully distinguishing the paper's contribution from the learning-augmented online algorithms literature and from other online fair division models (divisible goods, noisy valuations, temporal fair division).
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical or simulation component, even a lightweight one to illustrate the behavior of the proposed algorithms (e.g., Algorithm 1 or the frequency-prediction meta-algorithm) on synthetic instances; this could have made the contribution more accessible and would test practical tightness of the bounds beyond adversarial worst cases.

Several important cases are left as open problems without even a partial hardness or feasibility argument (e.g., the exact competitive ratio for PROP1 without information, and whether EF1 is achievable for n≥3 with frequency predictions), leaving key gaps in the overall picture the paper aims to construct.

The treatment of the 'identical valuations + frequency predictions' setting is dismissed briefly as trivially collapsing to the offline setting, without deeper discussion of whether this collapse is fully warranted (e.g., subtleties from not knowing arrival order versus needing to make irrevocable decisions per item as they arrive) or its implications.

There is limited discussion of the practical plausibility and acquisition of frequency predictions in real applications (how such multisets would be estimated or how errors/noise in these predictions would affect the guarantees), especially since the paper explicitly relegates robustness-to-noisy-predictions analysis to future work, weakening the practical motivation for the frequency-prediction model.

The presentation is very proof-dense with limited high-level intuition or illustrative examples accompanying the more involved constructions (e.g., Theorem 4.3, Theorem 5.1's meta-algorithm), which may hinder accessibility for readers not deeply familiar with online fair division techniques.

The paper does not discuss computational efficiency/runtime of the proposed algorithms (though they appear polynomial), which would be a useful addition for completeness given the algorithmic nature of the positive results.

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic treatment of online fair division across three progressively richer information regimes (no information, normalization information, frequency predictions), covering four standard fairness notions (EF1, EFX, PROP1, MMS) and their approximations, with matching upper and lower bounds in most cases, giving a fairly complete map of the achievability landscape (nicely summarized in Table 1).

Technically strong results with full, careful proofs: e.g., a novel algorithm using an 'outside-good certificate' that simultaneously achieves PROP1 for general n and EF1 for n=2 under normalization information, improving over prior MMS-only guarantees (Zhou et al. 2023) and shown to be a non-trivial extension via an explicit counterexample.

The meta-algorithm for frequency predictions (Theorem 5.1) is a nice general reduction: any offline 'share-based' fairness notion achievable in the single-shot setting can be lifted to the online setting with frequency predictions, immediately yielding the best-known 3/4+3/3836-MMS guarantee online, and further extended to an EFX guarantee for two agents via a leximin++ cut-and-choose adaptation.

Learning-augmented variants (noisy normalization information, noisy frequency predictions) are provided with clean, graceful degradation guarantees (additive for EF1, multiplicative for PROP1, and an explicit relative-error framework for share-based guarantees), connecting the work to the learning-augmented algorithms literature.

The paper is scholarly and self-critical: it identifies and corrects an error in a prior impossibility proof (Kahana and Hazon 2023), clearly delineates open problems (e.g., EF1 with frequency predictions for n≥3), and extends the study to the identical-valuations special case relevant to semi-online scheduling, deriving a tight golden-ratio-related EFX bound.
Random ized-algorithm extension (Appendix A) is handled carefully with a clean pathwise argument showing deterministic lower bounds transfer under the adopted ex post/adaptive-adversary model.
weaknesses: The paper is extremely proof-heavy and dense; the main text is largely a sequence of theorem statements and long adversarial constructions with limited high-level intuition connecting the many pieces, which may hinder accessibility and readability for a broad ICML audience.

The practical motivation (ad allocation, content moderation, recommendation exposure) is stated in the introduction but the technical content is a purely worst-case adversarial/competitive-ratio theoretical analysis with no experiments, simulations, or discussion of how well the idealized information models (exact totals, exact frequency multisets) correspond to realistic predictive pipelines beyond the noisy variants.

Some central questions are left open (e.g., whether EF1 is achievable for n≥3 with frequency predictions), and the paper only conjectures impossibility without resolving it, leaving a a gap in the otherwise complete picture advertised by Table 1.

The frequency-prediction model, while inspired by analogous notions in online knapsack/bin-packing/matching, requires knowing the exact multiset of future values per agent (including exact counts), which is a fairly strong assumption; although a noisy variant is given, the error model (Wasserstein-style instantiation cost) is somewhat ad hoc and its practical estimation from real predictors is not discussed.

The significance of the identical-valuations section, while theoretically clean, is a relatively narrow special case whose connection to the paper's main indivisible-goods motivation is comparatively weaker, and adds substantially to an already long and dense paper without corresponding gain in generality.

The presentation could better foreground unifying themes and proof techniques (e.g., the 'certificate' technique in Section 4 and the 'picking-sequence virtualization' technique in Section 5 are individually elegant but their relationship and reusability across the settings is not explicitly discussed), making it harder for readers to extract transferable insights beyond the specific theorems.

strengths: The paper provides a systematic and comprehensive treatment of online fair division across three well-motivated information regimes (no information, normalization information, frequency predictions), with a consistent set of fairness notions (EFX/EF1/PROP1/MMS) analyzed throughout, summarized cleanly in Table 1.

Theorem 5.1's meta-algorithm result is a genuinely elegant and general contribution: it shows any 'share-based' offline fairness guarantee can be lifted to the online setting given frequency predictions, via a picking-sequence simulation argument (Lemma 5.2/5.3), and this immediately yields state-of-the-art online MMS and EFX (n=2) guarantees.

The paper carefully identifies and corrects an error in a prior published impossibility claim (Kahana and Hazon 2023, Theorem 13) regarding PROP1, and substitutes a valid impossibility argument built on Benadè et al. (2018).

The learning-augmented extensions (Sections 4.1 and 5.1) are a natural and useful addition, giving graceful degradation guarantees under noisy normalization/frequency advice, and the paper explicitly discusses the interesting additive-vs-multiplicative distinction between EF1 and PROP1 robustness (Appendix B).
Proofs are highly detailed and appear internally rigorous, with careful case analysis in both the positive algorithmic guarantees (Algorithm 1) and the impossibility constructions.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical validation of any kind—despite motivating the work extensively via ML-driven applications (ad impressions, recommendation exposure, content moderation), there is no experiment, simulation, or case study connecting the frequency-prediction or normalization models to realistic data, leaving the practical relevance of the results largely asserted rather than demonstrated.

Several central questions are left open (e.g., whether EF1 is achievable for n≥3 under frequency predictions), which is an important gap given that this is one of the more natural questions raised by the paper's own framework; the paper only offers a conjecture without partial progress or bounds.

Much of the technical content (particularly the many impossibility proofs in Sections 3, 4, 5, and 6) follows a repetitive template of adversarial constructions with parameters (ε, δ, K) driven to extremes, which, while correct, offers limited conceptual novelty beyond variations of known adaptive-adversary techniques already used by Zhou et al. (2023) and Benadè et al. (2018).

The positive contribution in Section 4 (Algorithm 1) is presented as a generalization/modification of Zhou et al. (2023)'s algorithm; while the added EF1/PROP1 guarantees are valuable, the overall novelty relative to this closely related prior work is incremental rather than transformative.

The paper's fit to the ICML audience is unclear: apart from borrowing the 'prediction'/'learning-augmented' framing from the online algorithms literature, there is no learning component (no statistical/learning-theoretic analysis of how predictions are obtained, no online learning algorithm, no data-driven evaluation), making the contribution more suited to a game theory/EC-style venue.

The presentation is extremely dense and proof-heavy (many multi-page adversarial constructions embedded in the main text), which harms readability and makes it difficult for a general ICML reader to extract the key ideas without wading through lengthy case-based algebra; more intuition, illustrative examples, or proof sketches in the main body would substantially improve accessibility.

The identical-valuations section (Section 6), while thorough, largely re-derives known scheduling-style bounds and introduces a fairly narrow additional result (the tight (√5−1)/2-EFX bound for n=2), which feels like an appendix-level addition to the paper's core contribution rather than a central result.

strengths: The paper provides a comprehensive and systematic study of online fair division under three information regimes (none, normalization, frequency predictions), unifying and extending several previously disparate lines of work (Zhou et al. 2023, Kahana and Hazon 2023, Benade et al. 2018).

The results are technically strong and largely tight: positive algorithmic guarantees (Algorithm 1 for EF1/PROP1 under normalization; the general meta-algorithm lifting single-shot share-based guarantees to the online frequency-prediction setting) are complemented by matching impossibility results (e.g., EFX/EF1 impossibilities for n≥3, and the tight golden-ratio bound for identical valuations with normalization).

The meta-algorithm result (Theorem 5.1) is a nice structural contribution: it shows that essentially any offline 'share-based' fairness guarantee can be ported to the online setting given frequency predictions, which is a genuinely useful and generalizable insight rather than a narrow one-off result, and it is leveraged to obtain state-of-the-art MMS and even EFX (n=2) guarantees online.

The paper carefully engages with prior literature, correcting an error in Kahana and Hazon [2023]'s claimed impossibility and clarifying that Zhou et al.'s MMS algorithm does not satisfy PROP1/EF1, which shows scholarly rigor.

Learning-augmented (noisy advice) extensions are provided for both models with clean degradation guarantees (additive for EF1, multiplicative for PROP1), and the gap between the two is explicitly explained with a concrete example (Appendix B), reflecting good technical care.
The identical-valuations setting is a natural complementary special case connecting to the online scheduling literature, and the tight golden-ratio EFX bound for n=2 there is an elegant result.

The randomized-algorithm extension in Appendix A, though straightforward, closes an obvious question about whether randomization could circumvent the deterministic lower bounds under the adaptive adversary/ex post model.
weaknesses: The paper's threat model (adaptive adversary + exact ex post evaluation) is very strong, and essentially all the impossibility results (which form roughly half the paper's contributions) reduce to variations on 0-competitiveness arguments; while individually correct, this makes many of the impossibility proofs feel somewhat repetitive/mechanical once the pattern is understood, and the paper could better motivate why this adversary model (versus e.g., oblivious adversary or i.i.d. arrivals) is the most relevant for the stated applications (ad allocation, food banks, content moderation), where full adaptivity may be unrealistic.

Several central results collapse to trivial or vacuous statements under the adopted definitions (e.g., 'no positive competitive ratio' is achievable for many settings), which, combined with the paper's emphasis on 'tightness,' can make the overall message feel like it is mostly cataloguing which combinations of (fairness notion, information, n) yield exactly 0 versus something positive, rather than yielding a rich quantitative landscape.

The EF1 existence question for frequency predictions with n≥3 is left as an explicit open problem despite 'considerable effort' -- this is an honest and appropriate disclosure, but it does leave a notable gap in an otherwise fairly complete taxonomy (Table 1 has a '?' entry), which slightly undercuts the completeness narrative of the contribution.

The frequency-prediction and normalization-information models, while inspired by real applications, are somewhat idealized (e.g., exact knowledge of value multisets/totals) and the paper's discussion of how well these idealizations hold up under realistic estimation error is confined mostly to the additive/multiplicative degradation results, without empirical validation or any simulation to illustrate practical magnitudes of the guarantees under realistic error levels.

The related-work section, while thorough, is very long and could be more selectively focused; some subsections (e.g., Online Social Choice) feel loosely connected to the paper's core technical contributions and dilute the presentation.

Some of the long, case-heavy proofs (e.g., Theorem 4.3, Theorem 6.3) are dense and could benefit from higher-level proof sketches or intuition before diving into the epsilon-K construction details, which would improve readability without weakening rigor.
